1.pericope_label: Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity

schools.summary: Deal with the word before anything else, because the English will mislead the hearers all the way through. The noun is peculiar to the New Testament and a handful of Greek Old Testament passages and is not found in the heathen writers; "charity" now means tolerance or almsgiving, which makes the third verse absurd. Say so, restore "love," and move on. Then locate the chapter: three parts, the gifts worthless without love, love described, gifts transient against what endures. Note the oddity of its position, a hymn set in the middle of a controversial argument and coming from Paul rather than from John. Tongues are named first because that gift stood highest in Corinthian esteem and is really the least. The two closing figures need background rather than decoration: the tongues of angels answer to a rabbinic boast about a teacher who had omitted no branch of learning, the speech of devils and of palms and of angels included; the brass is a plate of metal that can only make noise; and the cymbal was two balls of brass struck together with neither measure nor tone, its participle the word used of the weeping and wailing round a deathbed.

Begin with an honest complaint about the text as received: the chapter division here is indefensible, the sentence that closes the previous chapter belonging with what follows and being completed by it, and a transcriber is the likeliest culprit. Then state the governing principle, that nothing is so excellent or estimable as not to be vitiated in the sight of God if love is wanting, and that this is no new doctrine but what the same apostle teaches when he calls love the end of the commandment. Take the gifts one by one as he does. Eloquence is an admirable thing considered in itself and does not recommend a man to God without love; liberality often proceeds from ambition rather than generosity; and martyrdom, the loveliest act of all, God still regards as nothing if the mind is destitute. Where love is wanting the beauty of all the virtues is mere tinsel. The rabbinic parallels are worth having here too, since the acts compared with love were the ones that nation esteemed most.

Put the translation question to the congregation as a plain contradiction: on the received rendering the apostle says that a man may have the utmost charity and yet not have charity. Give the history briefly, that the word came in from the Latin by way of Wiclif and was corrected by the earlier English translators before being restored. Then make the hypotheticals concrete rather than abstract. All the tongues on earth and the eloquence of an angel; the foretelling of future events; every mystery of the word and of providence; the highest degree of miracle-working faith; goods given away deliberately, piece by piece; the body surrendered rather than the religion renounced. Then say what the sum of it is: without this, whatever I speak, whatever I have, whatever I know, whatever I do, whatever I suffer, is nothing.

Warn at the outset against the common use of the word, which most men take for almsgiving; what is meant is love in its fullest extent, to God and to man, the living principle of all obedience. Then take the five things in order and give each its own sentence of application. A man might speak all the languages of earth with perfect propriety and it would be unharmonious noise; it is the charitable heart and not the voluble tongue that God accepts. A clear and deep head signifies nothing without a benevolent heart. One dram of love is worth more in God's account than all the faith of miracles in the world. There may be an open and lavish hand where there is no charitable heart, and the outward carriage may be plausible when the invisible principle is bad.

sides.position: No: the word now means tolerance or almsgiving, which destroys the force of the third verse; the Latin took it because the ordinary word for love was too fleshly, and the hope that English would grow into the larger sense has failed
No, and on the received rendering the apostle contradicts himself, saying a man may have the utmost charity and yet not have charity
No: the last revisers abandoned a sound correction made by their predecessors and brought back the Latinising word of Wiclif, who was excusable only because he translated from a Latin text
The Latin word is wholly inadequate
What is meant is not what most men understand by the word, namely almsgiving, but love in its fullest and most extensive meaning

debates.question: What does the last clause of the third verse read?

sides.position: "That I may boast": the reading of the oldest manuscripts, and correct
The manuscript evidence for the boasting reading is considerable, with Jerome and the Alexandrian codex behind it, and the copyists plainly did not know what to make of the received word
A strange reading that has crept into some manuscripts and weakens the passage, since what makes the sacrifice valueless is not a wrong cause but the absence of love
Burning is intelligible as written, though no Christian is known to have been burned as a martyr this early, Nero being the first

outliers.note: Alone refuses the chapter division itself, calling it so absurd that he could not refrain from changing it, since the sentence closing the previous chapter agrees with what follows and is completed by it; he attributes the fault to a transcriber.

Alone remarks on where the passage stands, finding it remarkable as coming from Paul rather than from John and as breaking into an atmosphere of controversy between stretches of close argument, which suggests to him a sudden and direct inspiration; he calls the chapter the baptismal service of love, the place where love receives its Christian name.

Alone supplies the rabbinic background to the tongues of angels, citing the boast that Rabban Jochanan ben Zaccai had omitted no branch of learning, the speech of devils, of palms and of angels included, and alone describes the instrument as two balls of brass struck together with neither measure nor tone, noting that the participle attached to it is the word used of weeping and wailing.

Alone gives the chapter a setting in sound, saying it comes like a sweet bell right between the jangling noise of the gifts in the chapters on either side, and that it is a pity to dissect the gem or pull the rose to pieces petal by petal.

themes: Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal
And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge... and have not charity, I am nothing
And though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing

4.pericope_label: Charity suffereth long, and is kind; envieth not, vaunteth not itself

schools.summary: Announce what kind of writing this is before expounding it: the apostle is attempting what he means us to feel is impossible, and he does it by alternating positive traits with denials of evil ones. Then take the words one at a time and give the congregation the lexical facts, since several of them are rare. The verb for kindness occurs almost nowhere else and may be the apostle's own coinage. The verb behind "vaunteth not itself" appears here for the first time in recorded Greek and comes from a noun for a braggart. The next is from the word for a bellows, so love does not puff itself out. The last of the group is a bookkeeping term: love does not enter the wrong in a ledger with a view to settling the account. Close by observing that the list is a portrait of the congregation's own faults reversed.

Slow the hearers down. Tell them not to pass the words over quickly but to weigh each one, so that they may see both the treasure in the thing and the art of the painter who has set the parts of virtue together like colours in an image. Then ask why long-suffering stands first, and answer that it is the root of all self-denial. Preach that at length and without moderation: it is more secure than a strong city, an invincible weapon, an impregnable tower; a spark falling into the deep does the water no harm and is itself quenched. Name armies, money, horses, walls and arms, and you have named nothing like it. Surround such a man with loss and you have not moved the rock; insult him and you have not shaken the tower; bruise him with stripes and you have not wounded the adamant.

Say plainly what the catalogue is for. It is not praise for its own sake but instruction in love's offices, and above all in how love preserves the unity of the church; and it is an indirect reproof, a contrast in which this congregation may recognise its own vices by their contraries. Where the commentators differ over a word, report the difference rather than choosing quietly: the term rendered "vaunteth not itself" is taken by most for acting precipitately and rashly, by others for foolish ostentation. Then press the diagnosis home. We are naturally so devoted to self that every man wishes to be carried on the shoulders of others and refuses to lend his own; the remedy is the love that makes us subject to our brethren. And when you reach "seeketh not her own," say what is not condemned: not every care for oneself, but the excess that neglects one's neighbour.

Number the properties and work through them one by one; the passage rewards a plain enumeration more than an argument. Render the first as having a long mind, to the end of which neither trials nor adversities nor provocations can reach, bearing the weakness and errors of the children of God and the malice of the children of the world, and not for a time but to the end. Take kindness as tenderness that creates trouble for no one. On the disputed word, take it that love does not act rashly and never passes a severe sentence on a slight or sudden view of things. Then let the section on unseemliness be as blunt as the sources allow: no ill-bred man is a Christian, and those who claim the name of blunt honest men and set themselves above civility have mistaken rudeness for candour.

Describe the grace so that the hearers may test themselves by it and, if they lack it, fall in love with what is so amiable. Set the two general heads first and hang the particulars on them: love is long-suffering, and love is kind; it is patient under injuries and inclined to do all the good offices in its power. Give kindness its own portrait — the law of kindness in her lips, her heart large and her hand open, not merely seizing on opportunities of doing good but searching for them. Then treat envy as the exact contrary, the effect of ill-will where kindness is the effect of good, and say the test: the prosperity of those to whom we wish well can never grieve us.

debates.question: What does the word rendered "vaunteth not itself" mean?

sides.position: From a noun for a vainglorious braggart; it means to play the braggart, and this is the earliest known instance of the verb
The learned cannot agree whether the word is Greek, Latin or Arabic; derived from the Arabic it yields "is not inconstant," but the sense is best given as not setting itself forward
Interpreters are by no means agreed; most ancient and many modern commentators explain it as acting precipitately and rashly
Love acteth not rashly: it does not hastily condemn, and never passes a severe sentence on a slight or sudden view of things

debates.question: How far does "seeketh not her own" go?

sides.position: It reproves not every care for oneself but the excess, which proceeds from a blind attachment to self and neglects one's neighbour
It is the Hebrew idiom of preferring one thing by affirming it and denying its contrary: love desires not its own welfare only, but its neighbour's also
Not ease, pleasure, honour or temporal advantage; and sometimes not even his own spiritual advantage, so long as zeal for God and for souls swallows him up
Simply its own interests

outliers.note: Alone treats the catalogue as a painting, with the parts of virtue laid on like colours and the members fitted together exactly, and alone presses long-suffering at length as the root of all self-denial -- more secure than a strong city, an impregnable tower, a spark quenched in the deep; surround such a man with loss and you have not moved the rock, insult him and you have not shaken the tower, bruise him with stripes and you have not wounded the adamant.

Alone reads the list as an indirect reproof, a contrast in which the Corinthians might recognise their own vices by their contraries, and alone states the diagnosis behind it, that being naturally devoted to self we grow morose and peevish, every man wishing to be carried on others' shoulders and refusing to lend his own.
Alone gives kindness its own portrait, with the law of kindness in her lips, her heart large and her hand open, not merely seizing on opportunities of doing good but searching for them.

themes: Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up
Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil

6.pericope_label: Rejoiceth in the truth; beareth, believeth, hopeth, endureth all things

schools.summary: The verse turns on two words and both are contested, so handle them openly. The first term paired against truth may be taken as unrighteousness or as falsehood; say which you take and why. The second, opening the next verse, comes from the word for a roof and has been rendered cover, bear, forbear and endure — the classical usage favouring the first, the New Testament usage the second — and the sense is not materially altered whichever is adopted. Then refuse the easy application. There are people whose real joy is in the triumph of evil, and men of the world take a malignant pleasure in hearing that a professor of religion has disgraced himself. Point out that the four verbs closing the verse gather the cardinal virtues and the Christian graces alike, and that love is presented as the queen of them all.

Turn the clause inward before turning it outward: the man who has this grace mourns the corruption of his own heart and the secret sins that none but God knows, and only then is he fit to grieve over other men's. Give the example from the gospels, the ear struck off in zeal for Christ and healed by him, where the injury was done for his sake and he was displeased by it. Then supply the qualification that the rest of the chapter needs and rarely gets. Bearing all things does not mean sanctioning vices by flattery or encouraging them by winking at them, and it does not exclude just punishment; believing all things does not mean that a Christian knowingly lets himself be imposed upon, or divests himself of prudence, or unlearns how to tell black from white. What is required is candour in judging — and it is better to be imposed on by one's own easy temper than to wrong a brother by an unfriendly suspicion.

Preach this one by naming the sins nobody thinks are sins. A man who has forborne revenge and left the matter with God consoles himself, when trouble falls on the offender, that his quarrel has been avenged: ask whether that is not rejoicing in iniquity. Interested people rejoice in the successes of an unjust war, their joy always in proportion to the slaughter, and call themselves Christians: say that if such Christians can be saved, demons need not despair. Then give the positive side its due, that those filled with this love rejoice in the spread of truth and therefore help it forward instead of hindering it. On the covering, be exact: whatever evil the lover of mankind sees or hears or knows of anyone, he mentions it to none, unless absolute duty constrains him to speak.

debates.question: What is the term set against truth?

sides.position: Falsehood, so that love rejoices in everything opposed to falsehood and irreligion, and therefore helps true religion forward rather than hindering it
Iniquity, the truth set against it meaning virtue, piety and goodness
Unrighteousness, with truth personified as its opposite
Injustice, so that love does not rejoice in any unjust action done even to an enemy

debates.question: Does the verb opening the seventh verse mean cover or endure?

sides.position: Cover, from the word for a roof; and Doddridge, Locke and Macknight so render it, though others make it forbear, the classical usage favouring the one and the New Testament usage the other, and the sense is not materially altered either way

Cover is urged because the common rendering merely repeats the endurance named later in the same verse; but the word will not clearly bear it, and to contain or keep in, as a vessel holds liquor, is better
Covers, protects and forbears at once, throwing a veil over a multitude of sins
Covers, but only after the offender has been privately and faithfully reproved and brought to acknowledge the fault
Covers absolutely: whatever evil he sees or hears or knows of anyone, he mentions it to none, unless absolute duty constrains him to speak

outliers.note: Alone names two ways of rejoicing in iniquity that pass for innocent: the man who has forborne revenge and then consoles himself, when evil falls on the offender, that God has avenged his quarrel; and those who rejoice in the successes of an unjust war, their joy always in proportion to the slaughter. Of the latter he says that if such Christians can be saved, demons need not despair.

Alone enters the qualifications the chapter's absolutes invite, that bearing all things does not mean sanctioning vices by flattery or encouraging them by winking at them and does not exclude just punishment, and that believing all things does not mean the Christian knowingly allows himself to be imposed upon, divests himself of prudence, or unlearns how to distinguish black from white.
Alone observes that the four verbs closing the verse gather up the four cardinal virtues of the Stoics and the three Christian graces alike, all exemplified there as marks of love.

themes: Rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth
Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things

8.pericope_label: Charity never faileth; we know in part, and we prophesy in part

schools.summary: Make the argument's structure visible: the case for love now rests on permanence, and the contrast is between things that are for a time and graces that are for ever. Note that the three verbs are not alike — prophecy and knowledge are to be rendered inoperative, while the middle voice used of tongues has them ceasing of themselves. Trace the verb for failing through its uses of stars falling, flowers fading and chains dropping from the hands. Then give the congregation a figure they can hold: gifts are the implements of the divine husbandry and graces are the seed, so that at harvest the tools are laid aside while the seed is transformed by dying and keeps that form for ever. On the timing, let the emphatic "then" do the work — the imperfect does not cease until the perfect is brought in.

Read the passage as pastoral strategy and say so. It is aimed in two directions at once: at those reckoned inferior, to persuade them that the chief of all signs lies within their reach so that they are not worse off than the holders of gifts but better; and at those whom the greater gifts had lifted up, to show that they have nothing without it. Envy is removed from the one and pride from the other, and a wall is thrown round the whole congregation. Reinforce it with the reasons already given them: the same Spirit is the giver, he gives to profit withal and divides as he will, and what he divides is a gift and not a debt. Though a man receive but little he contributes equally to the body, and the man with the greater gift needs him.

Correct a misreading before building on the text, because most people take "we know in part" to mean that our knowledge is not yet perfect and that we are daily improving. That is not the argument. It is because we are not yet perfect that we have knowledge and prophecy at all; they are helps to an infirmity, so when the infirmity ends the helps end with it, since it would be absurd for them to remain and serve no use. Guard the clause from three further misuses: it does not make the Scriptures incomplete and in want of traditions or fresh revelations, it does not confine knowledge to some of the saints, and it does not mean that only a portion of truth is known. On the timing, perfection begins at death but is not fully manifested before the judgment, so the whole discussion is misapplied when it is applied to the intermediate state.

Say what goes and what stays, in that order, and do not soften the loss. Prophecy and preaching, useful in their day, do not fit a soul for glory; the miraculous gift of languages ceases as unnecessary; and all human arts and sciences, however highly extolled here, are useless in the eternal world. One language will prevail among the inhabitants of heaven and the low imperfect languages of earth be forgotten. Give the comparison that makes it bearable: as starlight is lost in the light of the midday sun, so our present knowledge in the light of eternity. Then press the humbling of it — the man who knows most knows little beside what angels know, and the wisest of mortals will appear but an ape in the estimation of God.

Argue the preference from duration and be careful where the argument stops. Love is permanent and perpetual, lasting as eternity, while the gifts the Corinthians prized were to edify the church on earth and for a time only; heaven, which supersedes them, is the very seat and element of love. Then guard against the obvious misunderstanding. When knowledge is said to vanish away it does not mean that holy and happy souls will be ignorant, for a happiness that can consist with utter ignorance would be a poor one; what is in view is the knowledge supernaturally communicated. If anyone insists on taking it of common learning, then say that the way of knowing vanishes while what was learnt is not lost.

debates.question: What kind of knowledge is it that vanishes away?

sides.position: The knowledge supernaturally communicated, not common learning; the blessed will not be ignorant, for a happiness consisting with utter ignorance would be a poor one
All human arts and sciences, as being utterly useless in the eternal world though so highly extolled here
Our present knowledge, which is imperfect and obscure and will be lost in the superior brightness of heaven
The knowledge we now so eagerly pursue, which shall vanish as starlight is lost in the light of the midday sun

debates.question: What does "we know in part" assert?

sides.position: Not that our knowledge is imperfect and daily improving, but that it is because we are not yet perfect that we have knowledge and prophecy at all; they are helps to an infirmity and end with it
That our knowledge is imperfect and obscure compared with heaven, and should not therefore be valued as the gifts were
That knowledge and preaching are incomplete, and will cease when the complete dispensation is brought in
Not that the Scriptures are incomplete and in want of traditions or fresh revelations, nor that only some saints know, nor that only part of truth is known

outliers.note: Alone explains the passage as aimed in two directions at once, persuading those reckoned inferior that the chief of all signs lies within their reach while bringing down those whom the greater gifts had lifted up, so that envy is removed from the one and pride from the other and a wall thrown round the whole congregation.

Alone gives the figure of the husbandry, that gifts are the implements and graces the seed, so that at harvest the instruments however useful are cast aside while the seeds are transformed by the very process of death into blossom and fruit and remain in that form for ever.

Alone measures human knowledge against the angels' and quotes the epigram on Newton, whom superior beings watching a mortal explain all nature's law showed as we show an ape, adding that the poet took the thought from Plato without acknowledging the debt.

Alone notices that the verb used of tongues is in the middle voice, so that they make themselves cease or cease automatically, where prophecy and knowledge are made inoperative by another; and alone remarks how little of human work lasts.

themes: Charity never faileth: but whether there be prophecies, they shall fail; whether there be tongues, they shall cease
For we know in part, and we prophesy in part
But when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away

11.pericope_label: When I was a child; now we see through a glass, darkly

schools.summary: Correct the English first: the sense is not a moment of transition in the past but the present standing condition of a grown man, the verbs of childhood being imperfects and the becoming a perfect. Mention, without insisting on it, the suggestion that the three childish verbs answer one by one to the three gifts — speaking to tongues, understanding to prophecy, reasoning to knowledge — and that the number was at least made to match. Then take the mirror. Ancient mirrors were of polished metal and those made at Corinth were famous, and the word used means a mirror rather than a pane of horn or transparent stone, for which quite a different word existed. The following phrase is literally "in an enigma," and the point is exact: to see a friend's face in a cheap mirror is a very different thing from looking at the friend. Note the preposition repeated three times in "face to face," and that the last verb is the compounded one, to know fully.

Use the childhood figure the way it is meant, as an argument about education: much that suits childhood is done away at maturity, and so long as we are in this world we are under instruction, being far from the perfection of wisdom. Then answer the question the passage raises and few ask — what the mirror actually is. It is the ministry of the word and the means required to exercise it, which God, who is otherwise invisible, has appointed for making himself known; and beyond that, if you like, the whole frame of the world, in which his glory shines. The proof that this is right is what angels do not need: they have no use for preaching or sacraments, enjoying a vision of another kind. Say also what may be seen without the glass and what may not — God as the God of nature is legible in the works of creation, but not there as the God of grace.

Keep the childhood comparison concrete and unsentimental: a child has few ideas and little beyond instinct, and that less perfect than the instinct of the brutes, and no experience at all. Add that the putting away was done willingly and without trouble, which is the point of the figure. Then, if the mirror is to be discussed, give the evidence rather than an opinion — the ancient poet who called for his mirror to see how few of his hairs remained, and the brazen vessels of the Old Testament made out of what our version miscalls looking-glasses. The pastoral weight belongs at the end. Now the objects reach us as dim reflections and everything is a kind of riddle; then we shall see the objects themselves, and know in a manner in some measure like God's own, who sees at one glance through the soul and all things.

debates.question: Is the figure a mirror or a transparent medium?

sides.position: A transparent medium looked through, since reflection does not suit the obscurity meant; probably the thin plates of transparent stone the ancients set in windows
A mirror, and not a glass to look through; such an image would not have suited the apostle's design at all
A mirror: the same word is used elsewhere of one, and a pane of horn or transparent stone, though such were then used, would have required quite a different word
A mirror of polished metal, those made at Corinth being famous
A mirror, which reflects only imperfect forms in a dim and faint manner

debates.question: What is the mirror in the figure?

sides.position: The ministry of the word and the means required for it, which God, otherwise invisible, has appointed for discovering himself; and beyond that the whole structure of the world
The gospel: God may be seen in the works of creation as the God of nature, but is beheld as the God of grace only in his Son and through the glass of the gospel
The figure is of an object seen in a mirror far off, with blurred and undefined outline
The things that surround us, reflected so imperfectly that everything is a kind of riddle to us

outliers.note: Stands alone against the rest of the chapter's witnesses in taking the figure as looking through an imperfect transparent medium rather than at a reflection, supposing the thin plates of stone or mica the ancients used in windows, and supports it with a long account of the accidental discovery of glass by a ship's crew who rested their kettles on lumps of fossil alkali in the sand.

Alone asks what the mirror is and answers that it is the ministry of the word, the means God who is otherwise invisible has appointed for discovering himself, with the whole frame of the world besides; his proof is that angels, enjoying a vision of another kind, need neither preaching nor sacraments.

Alone documents the ancient mirror from the poets and the versions, quoting Anacreon told by the women that he is old and bidden take his mirror to see how few of his hairs remain, and noting that the brazen laver was made out of the very articles our version calls looking-glasses.

themes: When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child
For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known

13.pericope_label: Now abideth faith, hope, charity; the greatest of these is charity

schools.summary: Begin by refusing to read the opening word as a mark of time. It is logical, not temporal — the conclusion of the whole argument, not this life set against the next. Note that the verb of abiding is singular, agreeing with the first noun in the list, and that the closing adjective is comparative in form while doing superlative duty, the true superlative having grown rare by then. Then state the contrast the chapter actually draws, which is between ephemeral gifts and enduring graces, not between an imperishable love and a perishable faith and hope; popular hymnody has taught almost the opposite. There is no difficulty in faith continuing where he is seen face to face, nor in hope continuing if that life is progressive. Ground the primacy not on love lasting longer but on its mattering more to the welfare of others.

Take the verse as a summing up, and give it the figure of an account: when every deduction has been made, this is what remains. Note that faith is used more widely here than earlier, the whole ministry of the church existing to instruct us in these three. Then say the hard thing plainly, since the text will bear it: faith does not remain after death, the same apostle setting it against sight and making it last only while we are absent from the Lord, and hope is nothing but perseverance in faith, so both belong to a state of imperfection while love remains in perfection. Give the structural reason for the primacy as well as the temporal one — every man derives the advantage of his own faith and hope, but love extends its benefit to others — and specify which faith abides: not the faith of miracles, nor bare assent, but the faith peculiar to God's elect.

Resist the tidy formula that faith is lost in sight and hope in fruition, and put the question to the congregation as a question: does the apostle say so, or does any inspired man say so? Faith and hope will enter eternal glory as necessarily as love. Rest the primacy on likeness instead of duration. By faith we receive from our Maker and by hope we expect a future good, but by love we resemble him, for God is love, and by it alone are we fitted to enjoy him. Add the builder's figure — faith is the foundation, hope rears the superstructure, love completes and crowns it — and the decisive contrast, that faith and hope respect ourselves alone while love takes in both God and man. Love is called the fulfilling of the law, which is never said of the other two.

debates.question: Do faith and hope survive into the next state?

sides.position: No: faith does not remain after death, the apostle elsewhere setting it against sight; hope is perseverance in faith, so both belong to imperfection while love remains in perfection
No: the three are the sum of perfection on earth, and love alone the sum of perfection in heaven
Yes: the strain of the argument requires faith and hope to subsist where prophecy has ceased and knowledge vanished
Yes: faith and hope will as necessarily enter eternal glory as love will, and neither the apostle nor any inspired man says otherwise
Yes: the contrast is between ephemeral gifts and enduring graces, not between an imperishable love and a perishable faith and hope

Because it is the image of God in the soul: by faith we receive from our Maker and by hope expect a future good, but by love we resemble him; and love is called the fulfilling of the law, which is never said of the other two
Not because it endures longer, which the apostle does not intimate, but because it is more important to the welfare of others and a more eminent virtue
Because every man derives the advantage of his own faith and hope, while love extends its benefits to others; and faith is elsewhere called an effect of love, the effect being inferior to its cause
Because love is an attribute of God
Because even in the trinity of graces there is an order, and both faith and hope would perish without her

outliers.note: Alone complains that popular hymnody has taught almost the opposite of what was written, quoting the verse that has faith vanishing into sight and hope emptied in delight, and insists the contrast intended is between ephemeral gifts and enduring graces rather than between love and the other two.

Alone names the commentators ranged against him on whether faith and hope survive, and alone declines to ground the primacy of love on duration, holding instead that it is greatest because it matters more to the welfare of others.

Alone answers the formula that faith is lost in sight and hope in fruition by asking whether the apostle says so or any inspired man says so, and alone builds the primacy on likeness rather than duration -- that by faith we receive from our Maker and by hope expect a future good, but by love we resemble him.

themes: And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity
